blocks.text: Absolute electrode potentials cannot be measured because of the formation of an electrical double layer when an element is placed in a solution of its ions. When zinc is placed in a solution containing zinc ions, a tiny number of zinc atoms on the surface are converted to zinc ions, which go into solution, leaving an excess of electrons on the surface of the zinc. The solution around the metal now has excess Zn2+ ions, and some of these cations near the surface are attracted to it, so an electrical double layer is formed. This build-up of charge causes an electric potential (voltage) between the metal and the metal ions in solution (Figure 10.3).

Because of the double layer the potential cannot be measured directly, but the difference in potential between the metal/metal ion system and another system can be measured. This value is the electrode potential, E, measured in volts; the system used for comparison is the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE).

blocks.alt: Left: a grey zinc rod in zinc ion solution with minus signs along its surface and Zn2+ ions gathered beside it, labelled as the double layer. Middle: the standard hydrogen electrode with hydrogen gas entering a glass bell over a platinum electrode in 1.00 mol dm-3 H+. Right: a box of the standard conditions, the three half-cell types, the copper and zinc half-cells measured against the SHE at +0.34 V and -0.76 V, and the rules for reduction and oxidation at the terminals.
blocks.caption: The electrical double layer, the standard hydrogen electrode and the measurement of standard electrode potentials (original diagram after Figures 10.3 to 10.6 and topics 10.11 to 10.14).
blocks.long_description: A metal dipped in a solution of its ions sends a few atoms into solution as ions, leaving electrons on the surface; the ions crowd back towards the negative surface and a double layer forms, giving a potential that cannot be measured on its own. It is measured instead against the standard hydrogen electrode: hydrogen at 101 kPa bubbling over platinum black in 1.00 mol dm-3 acid at 298 K, defined as 0.00 V. Connected to a copper half-cell the voltmeter reads +0.34 V with copper the positive pole, because copper ions are easier to reduce than hydrogen ions; connected to zinc it reads -0.76 V with zinc the negative pole, because zinc ions are harder to reduce. Reduction happens at the positive terminal and oxidation at the negative one.

blocks.prompt: Explain how and why the electrical double layer forms (exercise Q.2a).
blocks.explanation: A few metal atoms at the surface lose electrons and enter the solution as cations; the electrons stay on the metal, making its surface negative, and the cations are attracted back to lie against that surface. The layer of electrons on the metal facing a layer of cations in the solution is the double layer, and the separated charge gives a potential difference whose absolute value cannot be measured, only compared with another electrode.

items: Zinc in Zn2+ solution: a few atoms dissolve as ions, leaving excess electrons on the metal; cations gather at the surface: an electrical double layer and a potential.
Absolute potentials cannot be measured; the difference from a reference, the SHE, is the electrode potential E in volts.
